title: AI Unlocked: Entrepreneurship & Growth
blurb: Beyond the launch: AI-native market research, operations automation, fundraising and pitch materials, growth engines, and an AI-leveraged operating model for founders scaling past themselves. (Launching from zero? Start with AI Unlocked: Entrepreneurship.)

modules.d: Running a growing business with AI as a force multiplier — without losing judgement, voice or integrity.
modules.body:
Beyond the launch

Launching a business proves you can sell. Growing it proves you can build a system: repeatable sales, reliable operations, healthy cash flow and a team or partners. AI changes how small businesses scale. Tasks that once required hiring — copywriting, basic analysis, customer response drafting, research, bookkeeping support — can now be handled by a founder with well-designed AI workflows. The AI-native founder designs the business so that AI handles the repetitive work and humans focus on customers, strategy, relationships and quality.

The founder's time audit

Growth usually stalls because the founder is the bottleneck: answering every message, making every design, chasing every payment. Track your time for one week in categories: selling, delivering, customer service, marketing, administration and finance, learning and strategy. Then mark each activity: automate (rule-based, repetitive), AI-assist (needs judgement but benefits from drafts), delegate (someone else could do it with a procedure), or keep (needs you — key relationships, strategy, final quality). Most founders find 30–50% of their week falls into the first three categories.

The leverage principle. Your goal is not to do more work faster; it is to multiply the impact of each hour. An hour building a reusable template, automation or procedure that saves ten minutes a day returns about 60 hours a year. Prioritise leverage over effort.

Where AI multiplies a growing business

  • Sales: personalised follow-up drafts, proposal templates, objection-handling scripts.
  • Marketing: content calendars, repurposing one piece of content into many formats, campaign analysis.
  • Customer service: FAQ answers, response templates, summarising feedback.
  • Operations: standard operating procedures (SOPs), checklists, supplier communication.
  • Finance: spreadsheet formulas, cash flow forecasts, pricing scenarios, invoice reminders.
  • Strategy: market scans, competitor summaries, scenario analysis and decision support.

What must stay human

Key customer relationships, negotiations, hiring decisions, final quality checks, ethical judgements and the founder's vision cannot be outsourced to AI. Customers can tell when they are treated as a process. Use AI to create more time for the human moments that build loyalty.

Risks of the AI-native business

  • Generic voice: AI content that sounds like everyone else erodes your brand.
  • Errors at scale: an automated message with a wrong price reaches every customer at once.
  • Data exposure: customer and financial data shared with tools without understanding their terms.
  • Tool dependency: building processes on a single tool that changes pricing or features.
  • Skill erosion: founders who stop understanding their own numbers or customers.

The founder's AI operating rhythm

Successful founders build a weekly rhythm: Monday planning (priorities and content), daily customer and sales blocks, a weekly review of numbers (revenue, cash, pipeline, customer feedback), and a monthly improvement session to automate or refine one process. AI supports each step; the founder owns the decisions.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my business operations coach. Ask me to list my typical weekly activities and hours. Classify each as automate, AI-assist, delegate or keep, estimate hours I could free each week, and rank the top five leverage opportunities by hours saved and ease. Then propose a weekly operating rhythm for me as an AI-native founder.

📚 Glossary

  • AI-native founder: founder who designs the business around AI-supported workflows
  • Time audit: tracking where working hours actually go
  • Leverage: multiplying impact per hour through systems
  • SOP: standard operating procedure
  • Operating rhythm: regular cadence of planning, execution and review

📖 References

  • Gerber, M. (1995). The E-Myth Revisited.
  • Mollick, E. (2024). Co-Intelligence.
  • Forteh, I. (2026). AI Unlocked: Entrepreneurship. Team21 Academy.

quiz.q: A founder spends 3 hours daily answering repetitive WhatsApp price questions. Which classification BEST fits this task?
opts: Automate or AI-assist with auto-replies, a catalogue and FAQ templates
Keep — only the founder can answer
quiz.x: Repetitive, rule-based questions suit automation and templates.

quiz.q: Building a template that saves 15 minutes per working day (about 250 days per year) saves approximately how many hours a year?
quiz.x: 15 minutes × 250 days = 3,750 minutes ≈ 62.5 hours.

quiz.q: Which activity should the founder KEEP rather than delegate or automate?
quiz.x: Key negotiations and relationships require the founder's judgement.

quiz.q: An automated broadcast with a wrong price reaches 800 customers. Which AI-native risk occurred?
quiz.x: Automation multiplies errors as well as efficiency.

quiz.q: A founder runs the entire business on one free tool that suddenly triples its price. Which risk does this illustrate?
quiz.x: Over-reliance on a single tool creates vulnerability.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of the leverage principle?
opts: Using as many tools as possible
Multiplying the impact of each hour through reusable systems
quiz.x: Leverage prioritises systems that return value repeatedly.

quiz.q: A founder no longer understands how her profit is calculated because AI prepares all reports. Which risk is this?
quiz.x: Founders must still understand their own numbers.

quiz.q: Customers complain that the brand's messages now feel robotic and identical to competitors'. What should the founder do?
opts: Refine prompts and edits to restore the brand's real voice, stories and customer specifics
quiz.x: AI should amplify, not replace, the brand's authentic voice.

quiz.q: Which weekly practice BEST supports an AI-native operating rhythm?
opts: Reviewing revenue, cash, pipeline and feedback once a week
quiz.x: Regular reviews keep decisions grounded in data.

quiz.q: Which task is a strong AI-assist candidate?
opts: Final approval of a large client deliverable
Drafting a personalised proposal from a template for review
quiz.x: Drafts that benefit from judgement and review suit AI assistance.

modules.d: Sizing markets, mapping competitors and reading customers — ethically and with evidence.
modules.body:
Growth needs a map

To grow beyond your first customers, you need to know how big the opportunity is, who else is competing for it, and what customers value. Market and competitive intelligence turns guesses into evidence-based choices about where to expand, what to offer and how to position.

Sizing the market: TAM, SAM, SOM

TAM (total addressable market) is the total demand for a product category. SAM (serviceable available market) is the part you can serve with your business model, geography and channels. SOM (serviceable obtainable market) is the share you can realistically win in the next few years. Investors distrust giant top-down numbers ("Africa has 1.4 billion people, if we get 1%…"). Stronger is bottom-up sizing: number of target customers × likelihood of purchase × price × purchase frequency.

Bottom-up example. A school-lunch delivery service in one Yaoundé district: 12 private schools × average 250 pupils = 3,000 pupils. If 10% subscribe at 15,000 CFA per month for 9 school months: 300 × 15,000 × 9 = 40.5 million CFA per year SOM in that district. Each assumption — schools, pupils, uptake, price — can be tested through conversations and pilots.

Competitive analysis

Map direct competitors (same solution), indirect competitors (different solutions to the same problem) and substitutes (including doing nothing or doing it yourself). For each, examine offer, price, quality, channels, customer reviews, strengths and weaknesses. A positioning map plots competitors on two dimensions customers care about — for example price and speed — revealing empty spaces you could occupy.

Porter's five forces help assess industry attractiveness: rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, and bargaining power of suppliers. Industries with low barriers to entry, such as many digital services, need differentiation and loyalty to protect margins.

Reading customers at scale

Customer reviews, comments and messages are a free source of intelligence. AI can analyse hundreds of reviews of your business and competitors to identify recurring praise and complaints — "late delivery", "friendly staff", "prices unclear". These themes reveal unmet needs and opportunities for differentiation. Combine with direct interviews and surveys, and track the jobs to be done: the progress customers are trying to make in their lives, which explains why they choose one solution over another.

Using AI for research — carefully

AI can summarise industry reports, suggest competitor categories, structure analyses and draft survey questions. But AI may invent statistics or describe outdated or non-existent competitors, especially in local markets. Use AI to generate hypotheses and frameworks; verify facts through primary research (visits, mystery shopping, interviews) and reliable secondary sources (national statistics, industry associations, reputable reports).

Ethical intelligence

Gather intelligence from public information, customers who choose to talk, and your own observation. Do not lie about your identity to obtain confidential information, induce competitors' employees to share secrets, or copy protected materials. Ethical intelligence protects your reputation and avoids legal risk.

From insight to action

Intelligence is valuable only if it changes decisions: which segment to target next, which feature to add, what price to charge, which message to emphasise. End every analysis with two or three concrete decisions.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my market intelligence analyst. For my [business] in [city/country], help me build a bottom-up SOM estimate with explicit assumptions I can test, a competitor map of direct, indirect and substitute options, and a two-axis positioning map. Then analyse the customer reviews I paste (mine and competitors') for recurring themes and end with three concrete decisions. Mark every fact I must verify locally.

📚 Glossary

  • TAM / SAM / SOM: total, serviceable and obtainable market
  • Bottom-up sizing: building market estimates from customer-level assumptions
  • Positioning map: visual comparison of competitors on two key dimensions
  • Jobs to be done: the progress customers seek when choosing a product
  • Substitute: a different way of meeting the same need

📖 References

  • Porter, M. (2008). The five competitive forces that shape strategy. Harvard Business Review.
  • Christensen, C. et al. (2016). Know your customers' 'jobs to be done'. Harvard Business Review.
  • Strategic and Competitive Intelligence Professionals (SCIP) — Code of Ethics.

quiz.q: A pitch claims: 'Africa has 1.4 billion people; if we capture 1%, we will be worth billions.' What is the MAIN weakness?
opts: Top-down sizing without realistic assumptions about who can actually buy
quiz.x: Investors prefer bottom-up estimates based on testable customer assumptions.

quiz.q: 10 offices × 40 staff × 25% uptake × 5,000 CFA per month × 12 months gives what annual SOM?
For a home-cooked meal delivery business, people cooking at home themselves are an example of:
quiz.x: Doing it yourself is a substitute solution to the same need.

quiz.q: Analysis of competitor reviews shows frequent complaints about late delivery. What opportunity does this suggest?
opts: Differentiate with reliable, guaranteed delivery times
quiz.x: Recurring complaints reveal unmet needs to address.

quiz.q: AI lists five named local competitors in your town, two of which you have never heard of. What should you do?
opts: Include them in the investor deck
Verify they exist and are accurately described through primary research
quiz.x: AI may invent or misdescribe local businesses.

quiz.q: Which practice is UNETHICAL competitive intelligence?
opts: Posing as a job applicant to obtain a competitor's confidential pricing strategy
Visiting a competitor's shop as a customer
quiz.x: Deception to obtain confidential information is unethical and may be unlawful.

quiz.q: Which of Porter's five forces is HIGH when it is easy and cheap for new businesses to start offering the same service?
quiz.x: Low barriers raise the threat of new entrants.

quiz.q: What does a positioning map help a founder identify?
opts: Empty spaces in the market where customer needs are underserved
quiz.x: Plotting competitors on key dimensions reveals gaps.

quiz.q: Which source is MOST reliable for verifying the number of private schools in a district?
opts: Education authority records or direct survey
quiz.x: Official records and primary research are more reliable.

quiz.q: How should a market analysis end, according to the module?
opts: With a long list of data
With two or three concrete decisions
quiz.x: Intelligence matters only if it changes decisions.

modules.d: Systems for sales, orders, customer service, finance and inventory — designed for reliability.
modules.body:
Operations are what customers actually experience

Marketing brings customers once; operations decide whether they return. Late deliveries, lost orders, inconsistent quality or slow responses destroy growth. As volume grows, informal processes that worked for ten customers collapse at a hundred. An operations stack — documented processes supported by simple tools and automation — keeps quality consistent as you grow.

Start with processes, not tools

Map your core processes from the customer's point of view: inquiry → quote → order → payment → delivery → follow-up. For each step, define who does what, the standard, the time target and the information needed. Write it as a standard operating procedure (SOP): a short checklist someone else could follow. AI drafts SOPs well from your description; you test and refine them with the people who use them.

The small-business stack

  • Customer relationship management (CRM): one place for every lead and customer, their history and next action — from a well-structured Google Sheet to dedicated CRM tools.
  • Messaging: WhatsApp Business with catalogue, labels (new lead, paid, delivered), quick replies and auto-replies.
  • Orders and invoicing: order forms, invoice templates or invoicing apps; mobile money payment confirmations recorded consistently.
  • Bookkeeping: daily recording of income and expenses; monthly profit and cash review.
  • Inventory (for product businesses): stock levels, reorder points and supplier lead times.
  • Scheduling: booking forms and calendars for service businesses.
  • Automation layer: Make or Zapier connecting forms, sheets, email and messaging (see the No-Code Builder Lab).
  • AI assistant: drafting replies, proposals, SOPs and analysis.
Reorder point formula. For stocked products: reorder point = average daily sales × supplier lead time (days) + safety stock. If you sell 12 bottles of juice a day, the supplier takes 4 days, and you keep 20 bottles as safety stock, reorder when stock reaches 12 × 4 + 20 = 68 bottles.

Customer service at scale

Build an FAQ from real customer questions; create response templates in your brand voice; set response-time targets; use labels to track open issues; and summarise complaints weekly to fix root causes. AI can draft replies and analyse themes; humans handle complaints, refunds and sensitive situations with empathy.

Quality control

Define what "good" means for each product or service — checklists, photos of standards, tasting or testing steps — and check before delivery. Track defects or complaints per hundred orders. Consistency builds reputation faster than occasional brilliance.

Measuring operations

Key operational metrics include response time, order fulfilment time, on-time delivery rate, error or complaint rate, repeat purchase rate and cost per order. Review weekly and improve one process each month.

Avoiding over-engineering

Do not build complex systems before you need them. Start with the simplest tool that works, automate the most frequent and painful steps first, and upgrade as volume justifies it. A clear checklist often beats an expensive system nobody uses.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my operations designer. I will describe my business and how orders flow today. Map my process from inquiry to follow-up, identify the three biggest bottlenecks or error points, draft SOP checklists for the two most important steps, recommend the simplest tool stack for my size, and propose two automations with triggers and actions. If I sell stock, calculate reorder points from figures I provide.

📚 Glossary

  • CRM: customer relationship management
  • Reorder point: stock level that triggers a new order
  • Safety stock: extra inventory buffer against uncertainty
  • Lead time: time between ordering and receiving supplies
  • Fulfilment time: time from order to delivery

📖 References

  • Gerber, M. The E-Myth Revisited — systematising the business.
  • Slack, N. et al. Operations Management.
  • WhatsApp Business — labels, quick replies and catalogue documentation.

quiz.q: A juice seller sells 20 bottles a day, the supplier takes 3 days, and safety stock is 15. What is the reorder point?
A growing caterer loses track of who has paid and who is waiting for delivery. Which tool addresses this MOST directly?
opts: A CRM or order tracker with status labels
quiz.x: Tracking leads, payments and delivery status prevents lost orders.

quiz.q: What is the BEST first step in building an operations stack?
opts: Map the core processes and write SOPs
quiz.x: Processes come before tools.

quiz.q: Complaints about wrong orders have risen. What should the founder do weekly?
opts: Summarise complaints to find and fix root causes
quiz.x: Root-cause analysis prevents recurring problems.

quiz.q: Which metric MOST directly measures reliability of delivery?
quiz.x: On-time rate shows operational reliability.

quiz.q: A founder buys an expensive ERP system for a business with 20 orders a month, and staff stop using it. What principle was ignored?
opts: Avoiding over-engineering — start with the simplest tool that works
quiz.x: Systems should match volume and complexity.

quiz.q: Which customer service task should remain human?
opts: Handling an angry customer requesting a refund for a spoiled event cake
quiz.x: Sensitive complaints need empathy and judgement.

quiz.q: What is an SOP?
opts: A short documented procedure someone else could follow
quiz.x: Standard operating procedures make quality repeatable.

quiz.q: Why does consistency matter more than occasional brilliance for growth?
opts: Reliable experiences build reputation and repeat business
quiz.x: Trust grows from consistent delivery.

quiz.q: Which WhatsApp Business feature helps track order status in conversations?
quiz.x: Labels such as 'paid' and 'delivered' organise conversations.

modules.d: Choosing the right money, building an honest, compelling pitch, and preparing for due diligence.
modules.body:
Not all money is good money

Funding should match your business's stage and model. Many successful small businesses never raise outside capital; they grow from profits. Others need external money to buy equipment, stock or reach scale faster. Raising money takes time, gives up control or adds repayment obligations — so choose deliberately.

Funding options

  • Bootstrapping: growing from personal savings and customer revenue — maximum control, slower growth.
  • Customer financing: deposits, pre-orders and subscriptions paid in advance.
  • Savings groups: njangi/tontines providing rotating access to capital.
  • Microfinance and bank loans: require repayment with interest, usually collateral or guarantees and good records.
  • Grants and competitions: non-repayable funds from foundations, governments and development programmes — for example the Tony Elumelu Foundation Entrepreneurship Programme, which has provided seed capital and training to African entrepreneurs. Competitive and requiring strong applications.
  • Angel investors: individuals investing their own money, often with mentorship, in exchange for equity or convertible instruments.
  • Venture capital: professional funds investing in businesses with potential for very rapid, large-scale growth — suitable for a minority of businesses.
  • Revenue-based financing: repayment as a percentage of revenue, available in some markets.
Equity is expensive. Selling 20% of your company for 5 million CFA values it at 25 million CFA after the investment (post-money valuation). If the company later becomes worth 500 million CFA, that 20% is worth 100 million. Only give equity to partners who add value beyond money, and understand every term you sign — seek legal advice.

The pitch deck

A strong pitch tells a clear story in about 10–15 slides: problem (who suffers and how much), solution (your offer and why it works), why now, market (bottom-up sizing), traction (customers, revenue, growth, retention), business model (how you make money and unit economics), competition and differentiation, go-to-market, team, financials (realistic projections with assumptions) and the ask (how much, for what, and what milestones it will achieve). Grant applications follow similar logic adapted to the funder's criteria, emphasising impact.

Using AI to build the pitch

AI is excellent at structuring your story, tightening language, designing slide outlines, anticipating investor questions, and building financial projection formulas from your assumptions. Ask it to play a sceptical investor and attack your pitch. But every number and claim must be true and evidenced.

Integrity in fundraising

Never inflate traction, invent customers, fake testimonials or present AI-generated projections as facts. Investors and grant panels conduct due diligence — checking records, bank statements, contracts, references and legal status. Misrepresentation destroys deals and reputations, and can constitute fraud.

Preparing for due diligence

Keep organised: business registration documents, financial statements and bank records, customer contracts or invoices, tax compliance, intellectual property, key agreements and team information. Good records also improve your own decisions — and are often the difference between businesses that receive loans and those that do not.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a sceptical investor and pitch coach. I will describe my business, traction and funding need. First, assess which funding sources fit my stage and explain the trade-offs. Then outline a 12-slide pitch deck, draft the problem and ask slides, build 3-year projection formulas from my assumptions, and list the 10 toughest questions an investor would ask. Flag any claim that needs evidence.

📚 Glossary

  • Bootstrapping: growing from personal funds and revenue
  • Equity: ownership share in a company
  • Post-money valuation: company value immediately after investment
  • Due diligence: investigation of a business before investing
  • Traction: evidence of market demand, such as revenue and customers
  • The ask: amount sought and its planned use

📖 References

  • Tony Elumelu Foundation — Entrepreneurship Programme (verify current terms).
  • Y Combinator — guides on pitching and fundraising.
  • Kawasaki, G. — 10/20/30 rule of pitching.
  • Feld, B. & Mendelson, J. Venture Deals.

quiz.q: An investor offers 6 million CFA for 30% of a company. What is the post-money valuation?
quiz.x: 6 ÷ 0.30 = 20 million CFA post-money.

quiz.q: A profitable tailoring business with steady local demand needs 1 million CFA for a new machine. Which funding option is MOST appropriate?
opts: Savings, customer deposits or a microfinance loan
quiz.x: Modest, asset-based needs suit savings, deposits or loans rather than VC.

quiz.q: A founder wants to show 2,000 customers in the deck when the true figure is 400. What is the MOST serious consequence?
opts: Misrepresentation discovered in due diligence destroys trust and may constitute fraud
quiz.x: Due diligence checks records; honesty is essential.

quiz.q: Which pitch slide explains how much money is sought and what it will achieve?
quiz.x: The ask specifies amount, use and milestones.

quiz.q: Which type of business is venture capital typically suited for?
opts: Businesses with potential for very rapid, large-scale growth
quiz.x: VC seeks large, fast-growing outcomes.

quiz.q: What is the BEST use of AI in pitch preparation?
opts: Structuring the story, tightening language and simulating tough investor questions
quiz.x: AI strengthens presentation and preparation, not facts.

quiz.q: Why should founders give equity only to partners who add value beyond money?
opts: Equity permanently shares ownership and future value
quiz.x: Equity is costly over time.

quiz.q: Which records MOST improve a business's chances of getting a bank loan?
opts: Financial statements, bank records and invoices
quiz.x: Lenders rely on verifiable financial records.

quiz.q: A grant panel's criteria emphasise social impact. How should the application be adapted?
opts: Emphasise evidence of impact and how funds will increase it, while remaining accurate
quiz.x: Applications should align with funder criteria honestly.

quiz.q: Customer deposits and pre-orders are an example of:
quiz.x: Customers' advance payments fund operations.

modules.d: Acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue — measured and improved systematically.
modules.body:
Growth is a system, not a campaign

Many businesses chase growth through occasional promotions. Sustainable growth comes from a system that consistently attracts, converts, retains and multiplies customers — measured and improved every month.

The AARRR funnel

Dave McClure's "pirate metrics" break growth into five stages:

  • Acquisition: how people discover you (search, social media, referrals, partnerships).
  • Activation: their first good experience (first purchase, first successful use).
  • Retention: whether they come back.
  • Referral: whether they bring others.
  • Revenue: how much value they generate.

Measure conversion between stages to find the biggest leak. If 1,000 people see your offer, 100 inquire, 20 buy and only 2 buy again, retention — not acquisition — is the problem.

Retention is the growth multiplier. Winning a new customer usually costs more than keeping an existing one, and loyal customers buy more and refer others. A business that keeps customers can grow steadily; one that leaks them must constantly refill a bucket with a hole in it.

Measuring retention

Repeat purchase rate: share of customers who buy again within a period. Churn rate: share of subscribers or regular customers lost in a period. Cohort analysis: track groups of customers who started in the same month and see what share remain active over time — revealing whether improvements are working. Net Promoter Score (NPS) asks how likely customers are to recommend you on a 0–10 scale; promoters (9–10) minus detractors (0–6) gives a score from −100 to +100. Sean Ellis's product-market fit test asks how customers would feel if they could no longer use your product; a commonly cited benchmark is that around 40% or more answering "very disappointed" suggests strong fit.

Growth levers

  • Referral programmes: rewards for customers who bring others — designed so both sides benefit.
  • Loyalty and subscriptions: recurring purchases and rewards for frequency.
  • Onboarding: making the first experience excellent so customers activate.
  • Content and community: educational content and groups that build trust and bring customers back.
  • Partnerships: businesses serving the same customers with complementary offers.
  • Pricing and packaging: bundles, tiers and upsells that increase revenue per customer.

Experimentation

Treat growth ideas as experiments: state a hypothesis ("A 10% referral discount will increase referrals by 30% in one month"), run it on a small scale, measure against a baseline, and keep or drop it based on results. Run one or two experiments at a time so you can tell what caused the change. AI can generate experiment ideas, draft messages and analyse results — the data decides.

Growth loops

The strongest growth comes from loops where customers' actions bring new customers: satisfied customers share photos of your product, which attract new customers, who share again. Design your product, packaging and service to make sharing easy and natural.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my growth analyst. I will give you my funnel numbers (people reached, inquiries, first purchases, repeat purchases, referrals) and monthly revenue. Calculate conversion between AARRR stages, identify the biggest leak, and propose three growth experiments with hypotheses, success metrics and baselines. Then help me design a simple monthly cohort retention table in a spreadsheet.

📚 Glossary

  • AARRR: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue
  • Churn rate: share of customers lost in a period
  • Cohort analysis: tracking groups of customers who started at the same time
  • NPS: Net Promoter Score: promoters minus detractors
  • Growth loop: cycle where customers' actions bring new customers

📖 References

  • McClure, D. (2007). Startup Metrics for Pirates: AARRR.
  • Reichheld, F. (2003). The one number you need to grow. Harvard Business Review.
  • Ellis, S. & Brown, M. (2017). Hacking Growth.
  • Reforge — growth loops essays.

quiz.q: 1,000 people see an offer, 150 inquire, 30 buy, 3 buy again. Which stage is the BIGGEST leak?
quiz.x: Only 10% of buyers return; retention is the weakest stage.

quiz.q: In an NPS survey, 50% are promoters, 30% passives and 20% detractors. What is the NPS?
A subscription business starts the month with 200 subscribers and loses 16. What is the monthly churn rate?
Why is retention described as a growth multiplier?
opts: Keeping customers is often cheaper than acquiring new ones, and loyal customers buy more and refer others
quiz.x: Retention compounds revenue and referrals.

quiz.q: A founder launches five new growth tactics in the same week and sales rise. What is the problem?
opts: It is impossible to know which tactic caused the change
quiz.x: Running one or two experiments at a time isolates causes.

quiz.q: Which hypothesis is BEST written for a growth experiment?
opts: Offering a 1,000 CFA credit to both referrer and new customer will increase referrals by 25% within 30 days compared with last month
quiz.x: It is specific, measurable and has a baseline and timeframe.

quiz.q: What does cohort analysis reveal?
opts: How groups of customers who started at the same time behave over time, showing whether retention improves
quiz.x: Cohorts show retention patterns by start period.

quiz.q: In Sean Ellis's test, what share of 'very disappointed' responses is commonly cited as suggesting product-market fit?
quiz.x: Around 40% is the commonly cited benchmark.

quiz.q: Customers post photos of a bakery's beautifully packaged cakes, attracting new buyers who post photos too. What is this?
quiz.x: Customer actions generating new customers form a loop.

quiz.q: Many first-time customers never return after a confusing first experience. Which lever helps MOST?
opts: Improving onboarding and the first experience
quiz.x: Better activation improves retention.

modules.d: An integrated operating model for growing your business with AI — strategy, systems, numbers and governance.
modules.body:
Bringing it together

Your capstone designs your business's AI Operating Model: how the business will create, deliver and grow value over the next 12 months with AI integrated into strategy, operations and growth — and with the governance to keep it reliable and trustworthy.

Components

  1. Business snapshot: offer, customers, current revenue, team and key metrics.
  2. Market and positioning: bottom-up SOM, competitor map, positioning statement and target segments for the next year.
  3. Founder leverage plan: time audit results and the activities you will automate, AI-assist, delegate and keep.
  4. Operations stack: process map, key SOPs, tools and automations with owners.
  5. Growth engine: AARRR metrics with current values and targets, retention measures and three planned experiments.
  6. Funding plan: capital needs, sources and milestones; pitch outline if raising money.
  7. Financial model: 12-month revenue, cost, profit and cash flow projections with explicit assumptions.
  8. AI governance: approved tools, customer data rules, review steps for customer-facing content, and quality checks.
  9. Risks: key business and AI risks with mitigations.
  10. 12-month roadmap: quarterly priorities, milestones and the dashboard you will review weekly.
The one-page dashboard. Choose 6–8 numbers you will review every week: revenue, cash balance, new customers, repeat purchase rate, conversion rate, average order value, on-time delivery, and one customer satisfaction measure. If a number does not lead to a decision, remove it.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit your AI Operating Model (no more than eight pages), the financial model spreadsheet, and the weekly dashboard template. Present a five-minute pitch of your 12-month plan to your mentor or cohort, who will challenge your assumptions as investors or partners would.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my business model architect. Using everything I tell you about my business, draft an AI Operating Model with the ten components from this module in under eight pages, build a 12-month projection with explicit assumptions as spreadsheet formulas, and design a one-page weekly dashboard of 6–8 decision-driving metrics. Then challenge my three riskiest assumptions as a tough investor would.

📚 Glossary

  • AI Operating Model: integrated plan for how a business creates and grows value with AI
  • Dashboard: small set of metrics reviewed regularly
  • Assumption: an estimate the plan depends on, to be tested
  • Roadmap: time-based plan of priorities and milestones

📖 References

  • Osterwalder, A. & Pigneur, Y. Business Model Generation.

quiz.q: Which dashboard metric is LEAST useful for weekly decisions?
opts: Total number of emojis used in posts
quiz.x: Metrics should drive decisions; vanity numbers should be removed.

quiz.q: Which component defines which tasks the founder will automate, delegate or keep?
quiz.x: The leverage plan uses the time audit.

quiz.q: A 12-month projection assumes revenue triples without explaining why. What should be added?
opts: Explicit, testable assumptions such as customers, conversion and price
quiz.x: Projections must rest on stated assumptions.

quiz.q: Which component addresses review of customer-facing AI content?
quiz.x: Governance sets tools, data rules and review steps.

quiz.q: Why present the plan to mentors who challenge assumptions?
opts: Because it is required by law
To expose weak assumptions before real money and time are committed
quiz.x: Challenge strengthens plans.

quiz.q: Which growth engine element should include current values and targets?
quiz.x: Funnel metrics need baselines and targets.

quiz.q: A founder includes 25 metrics on the weekly dashboard and reviews none. What should change?
opts: Reduce to 6–8 decision-driving metrics reviewed weekly
quiz.x: A focused dashboard is used; a crowded one is ignored.

quiz.q: Which risk mitigation fits 'automated messages could send wrong prices'?
opts: Review and test templates before sending and keep a single source of current prices
quiz.x: Testing and a single price source prevent errors at scale.

quiz.q: What does a 12-month roadmap provide?
opts: Quarterly priorities, milestones and review points
quiz.x: Roadmaps sequence priorities over time.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes the purpose of the AI Operating Model?
opts: To integrate AI into strategy, operations and growth with governance so the business grows reliably
To use as many AI tools as possible
quiz.x: It integrates AI into the whole business system responsibly.
